finding.claim: SQL injection through object keys when `permitSetMultiParamEntries` is enabled. An object parameter is expanded into `key`=value pairs. Each key is wrapped in backticks without escaping embedded backticks. Only the values are escaped. An attacker who controls the key names of an object passed as a query parameter can close the identifier and append arbitrary SQL. A typical case is an object built from a request body, such as `conn.query('UPDATE t SET ? WHERE id=1', req.body)`. A key like "a`=1, role=`admin" or "x`=1 WHERE 1=1 -- " changes the statement. The same flaw exists in the client-side `escape()` path.
finding.source: Keys of a user-supplied object passed as a query parameter (for example a parsed JSON request body) while the `permitSetMultiParamEntries` option is on. The option is off by default.
finding.sink: out.writeString('`' + key + '`') in the text protocol COM_QUERY packet. The client-side escape() helper concatenates '`' + key + '`=' at lib/misc/utils.js:213.

trace.note: permitSetMultiParamEntries is set from user options and is off by default
encoder.writeParam is called for each non-stream parameter
A plain object that is not GeoJSON and not toSqlString takes the permitSetMultiParamEntries branch
The key is written inside backticks with no escaping of '`'. Values go through writeParam, which escapes them.
The same unescaped key concatenation is in the escape() path (connection.escape and pool.escape)
batch-bulk text-protocol writes call the same encoder.writeParam

finding.guards_checked: Checked utils.escapeId at lib/misc/utils.js:91, which does double backticks. It is not called on this path. There is no key allowlist or regex validation. Value escaping is correct but does not cover keys. The option defaults to false, so only deployments that enable it are affected. Execute and prepared statements use the binary protocol and are not affected.
